field_notes.gcse_list: true when the word (or its headword) is on both the AQA 8652 and the Pearson Edexcel 2024 GCSE French lists, which the DfE requires to be drawn mostly from the 2,000 most frequent French words. A word on both is treated as a common high frequency word.
field_notes.dfe_annex_e: true when the word or its headword is on DfE Annex E, French required words (foundation or higher), Open Government Licence.
field_notes.gcse_ssc: the DfE Annex A French sound spelling links a sound covers. All 35 are taught by the end of Year 5 and secured in Year 6.
field_notes.recycled_words: spaced retrieval for the lesson starter and practice: words from 1, 3, 6 and 9 lessons before (about 1, 3, 6 and 9 weeks), so every word gets a long gap near day 60.
field_notes.carry_over_words: Year 3 words taught too late in the year for three recycles in Year 3; they open the Year 4 starters.

sounds.teacher_tip: Smile wide and keep it short and bright, with no glide at the end. The letter y says the same sound in il y a and stylo, which come later.
Round the lips and push them forward as if blowing out a candle. Children often read ou as the English 'out', so show the two letters as one sound card.
A short open 'a' as in the English 'cat', mouth wide open. It never says the English name of the letter.
Say 'ee', freeze the tongue, then round the lips into a tight circle. Fish lips is the cue. This is the sound English speakers find hardest, so praise the try.
Two letters, one quick sound: 'wa'. Hold up the oi card and say it with the arm doing a wave.

Most letters at the end of a word sleep and make no sound. Draw a little sleeping face over the last letter. Careful: c, r, f and l at the end usually wake up (avec, bonjour, neuf, il). Teach the word careful as the memory hook.
Say the French u, then slide quickly into 'ee'. Not an annex item on its own, but it carries huit and je suis, so it is taught early.
A nasal sound: air goes through the nose and the n is not pronounced. Children pinch their nose gently to feel the buzz. The n is a signal, not a sound.
Teacher note. A sleeping s or x wakes up as a z when the next word starts with a vowel: deux ans sounds like 'deu zan'. Children copy it from the audio; they do not need the rule yet.
Round the lips as for 'oh' and send the sound through the nose. Contrast with an: non and ans make a lovely pair.
Always 'sh', never the English 'ch' of church. Finger to lips as if saying shush.
A short smiley 'ay' with no slide at the end. The accent leans forward like a person walking towards you. Final er and ez say the same sound; that comes back with chanter and danser.
A more open sound than é, like the e in the English 'bed'. Three spellings, one sound: put è, ê and ai on one card. e before two consonants (sept, elle) says it too.
Say é, keep the tongue still and round the lips. Closed and small. The open version comes with sœur.
The final e is silent, but it wakes up the consonant before it: petit has a sleeping t, petite says its t. This is how children hear the feminine adjective, so it is taught with agreement.
Made at the back of the throat, like a gentle gargle. Practise with a soft 'grrr' first. Never roll it, never drop it.
The open eu, said with the mouth a little wider than in bleu. œu is a special joined letter; show children how to write it as o and e touching.
Always a plain 'k'. The u is silent after q, so qu never says 'kw' as in queen.
A buzzing z, the same as in English. Taught here because every number from 11 to 16 ends in ze and children try to say the e.
A quick 'y' glide into the nasal in sound. chien and bien rhyme, which makes a ready chant.
A nasal sound with the mouth in a wide smile. Four spellings: in, ain, aim, im. pain and vingt rhyme even though they look different.
The soft sound in the middle of the English 'treasure'. j always says it; g says it before e and i.
c says 's' before e and i. The little tail on ç lets c say 's' before a, o and u too, as in ça va. Children love drawing the tail.

sounds.grapheme: er, ez, et at the end
sounds.teacher_tip: The r of er and the z of ez sleep, so the ending sounds exactly like é. The t of et sleeps too. Every verb that ends in er is read this way.
One s between two vowels buzzes like z (maison). Double ss hisses like s (poisson, aussi). poisson and poison are a fun pair for the teacher, not the children.
A nasal sound. Many French speakers today say it just like in; children may copy either. The audio uses the common modern sound.
The short soft e in je, le and de, like the a in the English 'about'. In fast speech it often drops: samedi sounds like 'sam di'.
Three spellings of one closed 'oh' sound, with no 'w' slide at the end as English adds.
Another spelling of the open è sound. Group it with ai and ê on the sound card.
The l is not said as an l: eil sounds like the English 'ay' in 'say' cut short. It prepares for ille in Year 4.

sounds.grapheme: em, am before b or p
sounds.teacher_tip: Before b or p the n becomes m, but the nasal sound is the same as an and en.
ill usually says 'y' as in 'yes'. Watch the exceptions ville and mille, where ll is an l.
Before a vowel the nasal n is said and joined on: mon ami sounds like 'mo nami'. First heard in the Year 3 story.
A more open 'o' than in beau, as in the English 'pot' but rounder. Found in the middle of words before a sounded consonant.
h is always silent. j'habite shows it: the h does not stop the elision.
Like the ny in the English 'canyon'. One sound for two letters.
oin is oi plus the nasal in. oy before a vowel says 'wa' plus 'y'. Both extend the oi card from Year 3.
Never 'shun' as in English. The t says s, then the nasal on.
th is a plain t. No tongue between the teeth.
A sleeping t wakes before a vowel: c'est un sounds like 'say tun'. Taught alongside the first dictations.
ail at the end and aill in the middle say 'eye'. The last of the 35 GCSE sound spelling links, so the whole set is taught by the end of Year 5.
In ils aiment the ent is silent, so aime and aiment sound the same. Pupils learn to hear the difference from the pronoun, not the ending.
All three imperfect endings sound the same open è. Recognition first, spelling in dictation later.

grammar.point: Greeting people: bonjour for adults, salut for friends
grammar.teacher_explanation: French has polite and friendly ways to greet. Children say bonjour Madame or bonjour Monsieur to adults and salut to friends. Model both every lesson so the routine teaches the rule.

grammar.point: je means I and tu means you (one friend)
grammar.teacher_explanation: je is I and tu is you when talking to one friend or child. je becomes j' before a vowel (j'ai). The polite vous waits until Year 4.

grammar.point: Asking a question with your voice
grammar.teacher_explanation: Spoken French often turns a statement into a question by raising the voice at the end. Ça va. (falling) Ça va ? (rising). Children show the rise with a hand going up.

grammar.point: Saying your age with avoir: j'ai huit ans
grammar.teacher_explanation: French says I have eight years, not I am eight. j'ai and tu as are forms of avoir (to have). Saying je suis huit is the classic mistake; praise the j'ai.

grammar.point: Every noun is masculine or feminine: un and une
grammar.teacher_explanation: Every French noun has a gender. un goes with masculine nouns and une with feminine ones. Learn the noun with its un or une, never alone. Colour code: one colour for masculine, another for feminine, used all through the scheme.

grammar.point: The: le, la and l'
grammar.teacher_explanation: le goes with masculine nouns, la with feminine nouns, and both shorten to l' before a vowel or silent h. The gender learnt with un or une tells you which to use.

grammar.point: il y a: there is, there are
grammar.teacher_explanation: il y a is one fixed chunk that means both there is and there are. It never changes for plural.

grammar.point: Plurals: les, des and a silent s
grammar.teacher_explanation: Most nouns add s in the plural, but the s is silent, so you hear the plural in the little word in front: les or des. des means some, the plural of un and une.
examples: Il y a des sacs dans la classe.

grammar.point: Colours go after the noun
grammar.teacher_explanation: In French most describing words come after the noun: a red bag is un sac rouge. This is the opposite of English, so children say the noun first, then the colour.

grammar.point: Describing words agree: add e for feminine
grammar.teacher_explanation: With a feminine noun, most describing words add e. Often you can hear it, because the e wakes the consonant: vert, verte. petit and grand go before the noun.

grammar.point: my: mon, ma, mes
grammar.teacher_explanation: my changes with the noun: mon for masculine, ma for feminine, mes for plural. The owner does not matter, only the noun.

grammar.point: he has, she has: il a, elle a
grammar.teacher_explanation: il a and elle a are more forms of avoir. They are used for age too: il a dix ans. a has no accent here; à with an accent is a different word.

grammar.point: Building numbers 11 to 20
grammar.teacher_explanation: 11 to 16 are single words ending in ze. From 17 French builds the number: dix-sept is ten seven. The hyphen is part of the spelling.

grammar.point: he is, she is: il est, elle est
grammar.teacher_explanation: il est and elle est are forms of être (to be), the same verb as je suis. Use them with describing words: il est petit, elle est petite.

grammar.point: his or her: son, sa
grammar.teacher_explanation: son and sa both mean his or her. Choose by the noun, not the owner: son chien can be his dog or her dog.
examples: Elle a un poisson. Son poisson est rouge.

grammar.point: Likes take the: j'aime le chocolat
grammar.teacher_explanation: After aimer, French uses le, la or les where English uses nothing: J'aime la glace means I like ice cream.

grammar.point: Saying no: ne ... pas around the verb
grammar.teacher_explanation: To make a sentence negative, ne goes before the verb and pas after it, like two slices of bread. ne becomes n' before a vowel: je n'aime pas.
examples: Il n'est pas dans le jardin.

grammar.point: Joining ideas with et and mais
grammar.teacher_explanation: et (and) and mais (but) join two ideas into one longer sentence. The t of et is always silent.
examples: J'aime le pain et le fromage.
J'aime la glace mais je n'aime pas le gâteau.

grammar.point: aimer plus an action: j'aime jouer
grammar.teacher_explanation: After j'aime, an action word stays in its er form, the infinitive. J'aime chanter is I like singing.

grammar.point: Where little words go: beaucoup and aussi
grammar.teacher_explanation: beaucoup (a lot) and aussi (too, also) go straight after the verb, not at the end as in English.

grammar.point: Days of the week: no capital letter
grammar.teacher_explanation: Days start with a small letter in French. Use c'est to say what day it is: aujourd'hui, c'est lundi.

grammar.point: Weather with il: il fait beau, il pleut
grammar.teacher_explanation: Weather uses il with nobody doing the action: it. il fait plus a describing word, or a weather verb like il pleut.

grammar.point: Question words: quel and où
grammar.teacher_explanation: Question words start a question: quel (which, what) and later où (where). Quel temps fait-il ? is learnt as one fixed question.

grammar.point: du: some, as in il y a du soleil
grammar.teacher_explanation: du means some with a masculine noun. Learn il y a du soleil as a chunk; the full set du, de la, des comes in Year 4.

grammar.point: Instructions: écoute, répète, regarde
grammar.teacher_explanation: Telling one person to do something uses the tu form without tu: écoute (listen), répète (repeat), regarde (look). The class hears them every lesson.

grammar.point: your: ton, ta, tes
grammar.teacher_explanation: Works like mon, ma, mes. Used to ask about birthdays and families.

grammar.point: Dates: le plus number plus month
grammar.teacher_explanation: French says the three May: le 3 mai. Only the first of the month uses premier.

grammar.point: avoir mal à: it hurts
grammar.teacher_explanation: j'ai mal à plus au, à la or aux names where it hurts. à plus le becomes au.

grammar.point: Plural describing words
grammar.teacher_explanation: Describing words add s in the plural, usually silent: des yeux bleus.

grammar.point: er verbs with je, tu, il, elle: j'habite
grammar.teacher_explanation: Regular er verbs drop er and add e, es, e. All three sound the same; only the spelling changes.

grammar.point: Where things are: sur, sous, devant, derrière
grammar.teacher_explanation: Position words go before the noun, as in English.

grammar.point: Polite wanting: je voudrais, s'il vous plaît
grammar.teacher_explanation: je voudrais is the polite I would like. vous is the polite you for adults and for more than one person.
examples: Je voudrais un croissant, s'il vous plaît.

grammar.point: some: du, de la, des
grammar.teacher_explanation: some changes with the noun: du (masculine), de la (feminine), des (plural), de l' before a vowel.

grammar.point: Games and sports: jouer au, faire du
grammar.teacher_explanation: jouer à for games (au foot), faire de for many sports (du vélo, de la natation).

grammar.point: Telling the time: il est ... heures
grammar.teacher_explanation: il est plus a number plus heures. une heure is singular.

grammar.point: we: on and nous
grammar.teacher_explanation: on is the everyday spoken we and takes the il form of the verb. nous is the written, careful we.

grammar.point: aller: je vais, tu vas, il va
grammar.teacher_explanation: aller (to go) is irregular and very frequent. à plus le becomes au: je vais au parc.

grammar.point: How often: souvent, parfois, toujours
grammar.teacher_explanation: Frequency words go after the verb, like beaucoup.

grammar.point: Giving reasons: parce que c'est ...
grammar.teacher_explanation: parce que (because) plus c'est plus a describing word turns a like into an opinion with a reason.
examples: J'aime les maths parce que c'est facile.

grammar.point: Questions with est-ce que
grammar.teacher_explanation: est-ce que at the front turns any statement into a question, with no other change.
examples: Est-ce que tu aimes le français ?

grammar.point: Describing words before the noun
grammar.teacher_explanation: A few common describing words go before the noun: petit, grand, beau, joli, nouveau.

grammar.point: er verbs with nous, vous, ils, elles
grammar.teacher_explanation: The full present of regular er verbs. The ils ending ent is silent.

grammar.point: Comparing: plus ... que, moins ... que
grammar.teacher_explanation: plus ... que is more ... than, moins ... que is less ... than. The describing word still agrees.
examples: Le chien est plus grand que le chat.

grammar.point: être and avoir in full
grammar.teacher_explanation: All six persons of the two most frequent verbs, recited and used.

grammar.point: Near future: je vais plus an action
grammar.teacher_explanation: aller plus an infinitive talks about the future: je vais jouer.

grammar.point: Places: en France, au Canada, à Paris
grammar.teacher_explanation: en with most feminine countries, au with masculine ones, à with towns.

grammar.point: Building a paragraph: d'abord, ensuite, enfin
grammar.teacher_explanation: Sequence words link sentences into a short text for writing from memory.
examples: D'abord, je mange. Ensuite, je vais à l'école.

grammar.point: Daily routine: je me lève
grammar.teacher_explanation: Reflexive verbs have an extra me, te, se. Children already know je m'appelle.
examples: Je me lève à sept heures.

grammar.point: faire in the present: je fais, il fait
grammar.teacher_explanation: faire is irregular and very frequent, used for activities and weather.

grammar.point: Describing the past: c'était, il y avait
grammar.teacher_explanation: Two fixed past chunks for describing: c'était (it was) and il y avait (there was).

grammar.point: More negatives: ne ... jamais, ne ... plus
grammar.teacher_explanation: Same sandwich as ne ... pas: jamais is never, plus is no longer.
examples: Je ne mange jamais de fromage.

grammar.point: The past with avoir: j'ai joué
grammar.teacher_explanation: Perfect tense: j'ai plus the past form. er verbs end in é.

grammar.point: Past time words: hier, le week-end dernier
grammar.teacher_explanation: Time words signal the past and go at the start of the sentence.

grammar.point: can, want, must: je peux, je veux, je dois
grammar.teacher_explanation: These verbs are followed by an infinitive, as with j'aime.

grammar.point: il faut: you have to
grammar.teacher_explanation: il faut plus an infinitive gives advice for everyone.

grammar.point: The past with être: je suis allé
grammar.teacher_explanation: A small set of movement verbs use être. The past form agrees with a girl: je suis allée.
examples: Elle est allée à la plage.

grammar.point: Wishes: je voudrais plus an action
grammar.teacher_explanation: je voudrais plus an infinitive for plans and dreams.

grammar.point: Three time frames side by side
grammar.teacher_explanation: Past, present and future recognised and used in one short text, the hand over point to Year 7.
examples: Hier, j'ai joué. Aujourd'hui, je joue. Demain, je vais jouer.

units.title: Hello, who I am
units.context: Meeting a new friend at school: greetings, names, feelings, numbers to ten and age.

lessons.title: Bonjour !
i_can: I can say hello and goodbye in French.
I can say thank you.
I can hear the French sound i.
lessons.speaking_task: Walk and greet: pupils greet five classmates with bonjour and part with au revoir.
lessons.story_or_chant: Greeting chant to a clapped beat: « Bonjour, bonjour ! Merci ! Au revoir ! »

lessons.title: Je m'appelle
i_can: I can say my name.
I can ask a friend their name.
I can say hello to a friend with salut.
lessons.speaking_task: Name chain: each child says « Je m'appelle ... » and asks the next « Tu t'appelles comment ? »
lessons.story_or_chant: Puppet Bloop meets the class: « Salut ! Je suis Bloop. Je m'appelle Bloop ! »

lessons.title: Ça va ?
i_can: I can ask how someone is.
I can say I am fine or not so good.
I can make my voice go up for a question.
lessons.speaking_task: Thumbs survey: pupils ask three friends « Ça va ? » and answer with a thumb and a sentence.
lessons.story_or_chant: Call and response: « Ça va ? Ça va bien ! Ça va ? Ça va mal ! »

lessons.title: Un, deux, trois
i_can: I can count from one to five.
I can show a number with my fingers when I hear it.
I can spot a sleeping letter at the end of a word.
lessons.speaking_task: Finger flash: one child shows fingers and asks « Trois ? », the partner answers « Oui » or « Non ».
lessons.story_or_chant: Counting rhyme with actions: « Un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, salut ! »

lessons.title: Six à dix
i_can: I can count from one to ten.
I can say the numbers six to ten.
I can say the French sound ui in huit.
lessons.speaking_task: Number line up: ten pupils hold cards and the class counts them in and out of order.
lessons.story_or_chant: Rocket countdown: « Dix, neuf, huit, sept, six, cinq, quatre, trois, deux, un ! »

lessons.title: J'ai huit ans
i_can: I can say how old I am.
I can ask a friend how old they are.
I can answer yes or no.
lessons.speaking_task: Age guess: « Tu as huit ans ? » « Non, j'ai sept ans. » around the table.
lessons.story_or_chant: Unit rap: « Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Bloop. Ça va ? Ça va bien. J'ai huit ans ! »

units.title: In my classroom
units.context: Our own classroom: the things around us, what there is, and what colour it is.

lessons.title: C'est un livre
i_can: I can name a book and a pen.
I can say this is a book.
I can tell that un and une are two words for a.
lessons.speaking_task: Mystery bag: a pupil feels an object and says « C'est un stylo ? »
lessons.story_or_chant: Pointing chant: « C'est un livre ? Oui ! C'est un stylo ? Non, non, non ! »

lessons.title: Le livre, la table
i_can: I can say the book and the table.
I can sort words into le and la.
I can say the French sound ch.
lessons.speaking_task: Sort and say: pupils place word cards in a le box or a la box and say them aloud.
lessons.story_or_chant: Echo chant: « Le livre ! La table ! Le stylo ! Un, deux, trois ! »

lessons.title: Il y a
i_can: I can say there is a bag.
I can name a window.
I can find a new classroom word in a picture dictionary.
lessons.speaking_task: Classroom tour: pairs point and say « Il y a une fenêtre. Il y a un sac. »
lessons.story_or_chant: Look around rhyme: « Il y a un livre, il y a un stylo, il y a une fenêtre, un, deux, trois ! »

lessons.title: Des livres
i_can: I can say there are some books.
I can say what is in my bag.
I know the s at the end is often silent.
lessons.speaking_task: What is in the bag? « Dans le sac, il y a des livres et un stylo. »
lessons.story_or_chant: Bag song: « Dans le sac, dans le sac, il y a des stylos, dans le sac ! »

lessons.title: Rouge, bleu, vert
i_can: I can say three colours.
I can say a red pen.
I put the colour after the thing.
lessons.speaking_task: Colour hunt: pupils describe objects « un stylo rouge, un sac bleu ».
lessons.story_or_chant: Traffic light chant: « Rouge, non ! Vert, oui ! Un, deux, trois ! »

lessons.title: Une petite table
i_can: I can describe things in my classroom.
I can hear that petite has a t sound.
I can write a short phrase from memory.
lessons.speaking_task: Describe and draw: one partner describes « un grand sac noir », the other draws it.
lessons.story_or_chant: Mini reader page: « Dans le sac, il y a un petit livre vert. Il y a un grand stylo noir. »

units.title: My family and my pets
units.context: The people and animals at home, how old they are and what they are like.

lessons.title: Ma famille
i_can: I can say my mum and my dad.
I can choose mon or ma.
I can say the French r.
lessons.speaking_task: Family photo: pupils point to a drawn family and say « mon père, ma mère ».
lessons.story_or_chant: Finger family rhyme: « Ma mère, mon père, bonjour, bonjour ! »

lessons.title: Il a dix ans
i_can: I can say brother and sister.
I can say how old someone is.
I can say the sound in sœur.
lessons.speaking_task: Family facts: pupils turn picture cards and say « Mon frère a dix ans. Ma sœur a six ans. »
lessons.story_or_chant: Who is it? « Il a huit ans. C'est mon frère ! Elle a six ans. C'est ma sœur ! »

lessons.title: Onze à quinze
i_can: I can count from eleven to fifteen.
I can say qu like k.
I can hear the z sound at the end of onze.
lessons.speaking_task: Bingo: the caller says numbers 1 to 15 and pupils cover them.
lessons.story_or_chant: Number chant to a clapped beat: « Onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze ! »

lessons.title: Mon chien, mon chat
i_can: I can name a dog and a cat.
I can say what a pet is like.
I can say he is or she is.
lessons.speaking_task: Pet describing: « Mon chien est grand. Il est noir. »
lessons.story_or_chant: Chien and bien chant: « Mon chien ? Il est bien ! Mon chat ? Il est petit ! »

lessons.title: Son poisson
i_can: I can say his fish or her fish.
I can choose son or sa.
I can read a short sentence about a pet.
lessons.speaking_task: Guess the owner: « C'est le poisson de Léa ? Oui, c'est son poisson. »
lessons.story_or_chant: Mini reader page: « C'est Léa. Elle a un poisson. Son poisson est rouge. »

lessons.title: Jusqu'à vingt
i_can: I can count to twenty.
I can present my family or pets to the class.
I can write a sentence about my family from memory.
lessons.speaking_task: Show and tell: each pupil presents a drawing « C'est mon chien. Il est petit. Il a onze ans. »
lessons.story_or_chant: Twenty clap: count to twenty, clapping only on the numbers with a nasal sound.

units.title: What I like
units.context: Food and play at home and at school: what we like, what we do not like, and why not both.

lessons.title: J'aime la glace
i_can: I can say what I like.
I can ask a friend what they like.
I know French says I like the ice cream.
lessons.speaking_task: Likes survey: « Tu aimes la glace ? » « Oui, j'aime la glace ! »
lessons.story_or_chant: Ice cream chant: « J'aime, j'aime, j'aime la glace ! Tu aimes la glace ? »

lessons.title: Je n'aime pas
i_can: I can say what I do not like.
I can put ne and pas around the verb.
I can say a soft c.
lessons.speaking_task: Thumbs up or down: pupils react to picture cards with « J'aime » or « Je n'aime pas ».
lessons.story_or_chant: Sandwich chant with hand actions for ne and pas: « Je n'aime pas, je n'aime pas, je n'aime pas le fromage ! »

lessons.title: Et, mais
i_can: I can join two likes with et.
I can say I like one thing but not another.
I can write a longer sentence from memory.
lessons.speaking_task: Sentence builder: partners spin a food wheel and say « J'aime le pain mais je n'aime pas le fromage. »
lessons.story_or_chant: Lunchbox rhyme: « Le pain et le fromage, le gâteau et la glace, merci ! »

lessons.title: La musique, le foot
i_can: I can say I like football or music.
I can read like and dislike sentences.
I can work out a new word from a picture.
lessons.speaking_task: Four corners: corners are le foot, la musique, la télé, le gâteau; pupils go to one and say why.
lessons.story_or_chant: Read and match: short speech bubbles « J'aime la télé mais je n'aime pas le foot. » matched to children.

lessons.title: J'aime chanter
i_can: I can say I like playing, singing and dancing.
I can read er at the end as é.
I can join in a French action song.
lessons.speaking_task: Action mime: a pupil mimes, the class guesses « Tu aimes danser ? »
lessons.story_or_chant: Action song: « J'aime chanter, j'aime danser, j'aime jouer, oui, oui, oui ! »

lessons.title: J'aime beaucoup lire
i_can: I can say I like something a lot.
I can say I like something too.
I can write three sentences about my likes.
lessons.speaking_task: Likes card: pupils present three sentences to a small group.
lessons.story_or_chant: Likes poem: « J'aime beaucoup lire. J'aime aussi chanter. J'aime beaucoup, beaucoup la glace ! »

units.title: My week and the weather
units.context: A class weather diary: what day it is, what the sky is doing, and what we like to do.

lessons.title: Lundi, mardi, mercredi
i_can: I can say three days of the week.
I can say what day it is today.
I can say the sound un in lundi.
lessons.speaking_task: Calendar helper: the daily helper says « Aujourd'hui, c'est lundi. »
lessons.story_or_chant: Days song, first half: « Lundi, mardi, mercredi, aujourd'hui, c'est lundi ! »

lessons.title: Jeudi à dimanche
i_can: I can say all the days of the week.
I can write the days with a small letter.
I can sing the days song.
lessons.speaking_task: Day relay: pupils say the days in order around the circle, then backwards.
lessons.story_or_chant: Days song, full: seven days to a familiar tune, clapping on dimanche.

lessons.title: Il fait beau
i_can: I can say the weather is nice.
I can say it is hot or cold.
I can say the sound in beau and chaud.
lessons.speaking_task: Weather window: pupils look outside and report « Il fait froid ! »
lessons.story_or_chant: Weather actions: « Il fait chaud » (fan face), « Il fait froid » (shiver), « Il fait beau » (big smile).

lessons.title: Quel temps fait-il ?
i_can: I can ask what the weather is like.
I can say it is raining or snowing.
I can make my question sound like a question.
lessons.speaking_task: Weather reporter: one pupil asks « Quel temps fait-il ? », the reporter answers from a picture card.
lessons.story_or_chant: Rain rhyme: « Il pleut, il pleut, il neige, il neige, il fait froid ! »

lessons.title: Demain, il y a du soleil
i_can: I can say what the weather will be tomorrow.
I can say there is sun.
I can read a short weather report.
lessons.speaking_task: TV forecast: pairs present a forecast to the class from a map « Lundi, il pleut. Mardi, il y a du soleil. »
lessons.story_or_chant: Forecast reader: « Aujourd'hui, il fait froid. Demain, il y a du soleil ! »

lessons.title: Ma semaine
i_can: I can write about my week from memory.
I can say what I like doing at the weekend.
I can use a word list to check a spelling.
lessons.speaking_task: My week poster: pupils describe one day « Samedi, il fait beau. J'aime jouer. »
lessons.story_or_chant: Weekend poem: « Le week-end, samedi, dimanche, j'aime le week-end ! »

units.title: Our story
units.context: The class story of Bloop, Pebble and a missing cat, read, acted and performed, then the end of year check.

lessons.title: Voici ma maison
i_can: I can read the first page of our story.
I can say here is my house.
I can read a story aloud with a partner.
lessons.speaking_task: Paired reading: partners read page one aloud, one sentence each.
lessons.story_or_chant: Story page 1: « Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Bloop. Voici ma maison. Voici mon ami Pebble. Il est petit et il est vert. »

lessons.title: Où est le chat ?
i_can: I can ask where something is.
I can say look!
I can follow what happens in the story.
lessons.speaking_task: Hide and seek: a toy cat is hidden; pupils ask « Où est le chat ? Il est dans le sac ? »
lessons.story_or_chant: Story page 2: « Voici mon chat. Il est noir. Regarde ! Où est le chat ? Il est dans le jardin ? Non ! »

lessons.title: Triste, content
i_can: I can say how a character feels.
I can hear content and contente.
I can read a page with feeling.
lessons.speaking_task: Feelings freeze frame: groups act a moment of the story and say how the character feels.
lessons.story_or_chant: Story page 3: « Bloop est triste. Il pleut. Il fait froid. Pebble regarde dans la maison. Le chat est ici, dans le sac rouge ! Bloop est content. »

lessons.title: Ensemble !
i_can: I can read the end of the story.
I can rehearse my lines with my group.
I can join in when we say a line together.
lessons.speaking_task: Rehearsal: groups of four practise the story, each with a part and a chorus line.
lessons.story_or_chant: Story page 4: « Ensemble ! Il y a du gâteau. J'aime le gâteau ! Encore ! La fin. »

lessons.title: Le spectacle
i_can: I can perform our story to an audience.
I can speak clearly so others understand.
I can follow French instructions.
lessons.speaking_task: Performance: each group performs the story for another class or for parents.
lessons.story_or_chant: Warm up chant: « Écoute ! Répète ! C'est facile ! Encore ! »

lessons.title: Bonnes vacances
i_can: I can show what I have learnt this year.
I can write about me from memory.
I can say see you soon.
lessons.speaking_task: End of year check: a short conversation with the teacher (name, age, likes, weather) plus a read aloud.
lessons.story_or_chant: Last page: « C'est l'été. Il fait beau. Les vacances ! Au revoir et à bientôt ! »
